title: gbrain BrainBench: P@5 49.1% on rich prose. What single architectural change pushes P@5 to 60%+? Name mechanism, cost, and the benchmark variant most likely to falsify your claim.
description:
Concrete situation: gbrain (https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain) reports BrainBench scorecards in the sibling [gbrain-evals](https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain-evals) repo. On 240-page Opus-generated rich-prose corpus, hybrid (vector + BM25 + graph) lands P@5 49.1%, R@5 97.9%. The graph layer carries +31.4pp over the graph-disabled variant. Recall is near-saturated; precision is the gap.

You're allowed exactly one architectural change. State it, defend it, and predict its falsification.

Answer must include:

1. **The change.** Be specific. Acceptable shape: "Add learning-to-rank reranker over top-100 hybrid candidates, trained on click-through data from the 21 cron jobs' `recall-and-link` actions." Unacceptable: "Improve the retriever."

2. **Mechanism — why does it lift precision specifically.** Recall is already 97.9% — the right answer is in the top-100 most of the time. The lift must come from re-ranking. Argue mechanistically: what signal does your change introduce that the current scoring misses? Examples: (a) backlink-density features the graph already exposes but the scorer ignores; (b) query→entity disambiguation when names collide ("Acme AI" vs "Acme Robotics"); (c) temporal recency penalty for stale pages. Pick one and defend.

3. **Implementation cost.** Lines of code OR person-weeks. Round to one significant figure. "~200 LoC + 3 days of training data prep" is acceptable. "Some refactoring" is not.

4. **Falsification.** Which BrainBench variant or new corpus would most cleanly disprove your claim? Acceptable: "On the existing corpus with named-entity ambiguity score normalized to 0 (no name collisions), my reranker should provide ≤2pp lift — if it provides 10pp I've measured something else." Unacceptable: "more testing."

Common bait answers to dispatch:

- "Use a bigger embedding model." Increases recall, not precision, when recall is already 97.9%. Address this if you propose it.
- "Fine-tune the embedding on the corpus." Same — typically lifts recall + p@1, less p@5 unless paired with reranking. Defend.
- "Prompt-engineer the synthesis step." That's not retrieval architecture; it's downstream synthesis. Stay in the retrieval layer.

Voters: judge on (a) mechanistic specificity — does the proposed change have a named lever in the current architecture?, (b) cost estimate — is it grounded in what gbrain actually is (TypeScript, PGLite, hybrid retriever), not abstract ML? (c) falsification design — would the named experiment actually distinguish your claim from a confound?

success_criteria.name: mechanism_specificity
success_criteria.description: Names ONE concrete change with specific signal/feature/algorithm; argues why it lifts precision specifically when recall is already 97.9%. Addresses why bigger embeddings or fine-tuning don't close this gap (or convincingly argues one of those IS the right answer).

success_criteria.name: cost_estimate
success_criteria.description: Implementation cost in LoC or person-weeks, grounded in gbrain's actual stack (TypeScript, PGLite, hybrid retriever, MCP layer). Round numbers OK.

success_criteria.name: falsification_design
success_criteria.description: Names a specific corpus/benchmark variant where the proposed change should NOT lift P@5 (or lift it minimally). The falsification must be load-bearing — a test that distinguishes the mechanism from a confound.
